questions.question: Explain NoSQL fundamentals — CAP, BASE, consistency models, and when to use each category.
questions.title: NoSQL Fundamentals: CAP, BASE, Consistency Models
questions.direct_answer: NoSQL is not one thing — it is **four data-model families** (key-value, document, wide-column, graph) that each relax a SQL guarantee to gain horizontal scale, flexible schema, or access-pattern speed. **CAP** says during a partition you pick consistency or availability; **PACELC** adds: even without partitions you trade latency for consistency. **BASE** (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) is the NoSQL philosophy opposing ACID. Most modern NoSQL offers **tunable consistency** — Cassandra consistency levels, DynamoDB strong-reads, MongoDB read/write concerns. The real skill is matching access patterns to the right store — Postgres in 2026 covers many cases people historically reached for NoSQL to solve.

interviewer_intent.testing: Conceptual understanding of NoSQL theory and practical selection across the four data-model families
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating CAP as a daily trade-off, calling all NoSQL 'eventually consistent', ignoring PACELC's latency-consistency trade-off, and assuming NoSQL always scales better than SQL
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss PACELC, tunable consistency, BASE vs ACID in practice, quorum math (W + R > N), and the 2026 Postgres JSONB shift that closed many NoSQL gaps

sections.title: What NoSQL Actually Is
sections.content:
'NoSQL' was coined at a 2009 meetup — originally meaning **'not only SQL'**, a rejection of 'one DB fits all', not a rejection of SQL. In practice, NoSQL is a family of stores that each relax one or more SQL guarantees to gain something specific: horizontal scale, flexible schema, or blazing-fast access for one pattern.

The **four families** are key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), document (MongoDB, Couchbase), wide-column (Cassandra, ScyllaDB), and graph (Neo4j, Neptune). Each shines at a narrow set of access patterns and performs poorly outside them.

By 2026, **Postgres with JSONB, full-text, pgvector, and logical replication** closes many historical NoSQL gaps. The mature selection question is no longer 'SQL or NoSQL' but 'which store fits this specific access pattern best'.

sections.title: CAP Theorem and Network Partitions
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph normal["Normal Operation"]
        nodeA["Node A"] <--> nodeB["Node B"]
        nodeA <--> nodeC["Node C"]
        clientN["Client"] --> nodeA
    end
    subgraph partition["Network Partition: A+B | C"]
        partA["Node A"] <--> partB["Node B"]
        partA -.X.- partC["Node C (isolated)"]
        clientP["Client"] --> partC
    end
    subgraph choice["Choice During Partition"]
        writer["Client writes to C"]
        writer --> cpChoice["CP: refuse write / error (Postgres, CockroachDB)"]
        writer --> apChoice["AP: accept write, reconcile later (Cassandra, DynamoDB)"]
    end
```

sections.title: The Four NoSQL Families
sections.content:
**Key-Value stores (Redis, DynamoDB, Riak)**
- O(1) lookup by key; values are opaque blobs or typed (string, hash, list, set)
- Fastest, simplest model
- Use for: cache, sessions, rate limits, feature flags, lookup-by-id
- Weak at: range scans, ad-hoc queries, cross-key joins

**Document stores (MongoDB, Couchbase, DocumentDB)**
- JSON-like documents in collections; schema-flexible per document
- Rich query on nested fields, aggregation pipeline, secondary indexes
- Use for: CMS, product catalogs, user profiles, event records with varying shape
- Weak at: multi-document transactions (better since 4.0 but costly), heavy joins

**Wide-column stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, BigTable)**
- Tables with flexible columns per row; partitioned by row key
- Optimized for writes; eventually consistent by default; tunable consistency
- Use for: time-series, IoT telemetry, event logs, massive write throughput
- Weak at: ad-hoc queries not anticipated in schema, deletes (tombstones)

**Graph stores (Neo4j, Neptune, TigerGraph)**
- Nodes + edges; optimized for multi-hop traversal
- Use for: social graphs, fraud detection, recommendations, knowledge graphs
- Weak at: large tabular scans, heavy aggregation

sections.title: CAP and PACELC Explained
sections.content:
**CAP theorem (Eric Brewer, 2000)**
- During a network **partition**, you can have at most two of: **Consistency**, **Availability**, **Partition tolerance**
- Partitions happen; P is mandatory in distributed systems
- So the real choice is **CP or AP during partition**

**Classifications**
- CP: Postgres HA, MongoDB primary, Spanner, CockroachDB, HBase
- AP: Cassandra (default), DynamoDB (default), Riak

```javascript
// MongoDB — CP behavior: if primary unreachable, writes fail until new primary elected
db.orders.insertOne({ _id: 1, total: 99 }, { writeConcern: { w: "majority" } });
// During partition of minority side, this throws NotWritablePrimary

// Cassandra — AP: still writes locally with CL=ONE even during partition
// Later, hinted handoff + read repair reconciles
```

**PACELC (Daniel Abadi, 2010) — more practical**
- In **P**artition: choose **A** or **C** (like CAP)
- **E**lse (normal operation): choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency

**Classifications under PACELC**
- Cassandra: PA/EL — available during partition, latency over consistency normally
- Spanner, CockroachDB: PC/EC — strong consistency always, at latency cost
- DynamoDB default: PA/EL
- MongoDB: PC/EC when using majority read/write concerns

sections.title: Consistency Models and Quorum Math
NoSQL Myths and Real Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When NoSQL helps:**
- Access pattern genuinely KV or document-first
- Massive write throughput (100K+ writes/sec) — Cassandra/Scylla
- AWS serverless + auto-scale without ops — DynamoDB
- Graph-heavy queries — Neo4j
- Rapidly varying document shapes — MongoDB (or Postgres JSONB)

**When NoSQL hurts:**
- Data is genuinely relational (orders ↔ line items ↔ products)
- Ad-hoc analytical queries required
- Small scale — operational cost exceeds benefit
- Team lacks NoSQL operational expertise

**Myths to dispel:**
- 'NoSQL is faster' — only for its intended access pattern; Postgres often wins on indexed queries
- 'NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't' — single-node Postgres handles 10TB+; Aurora, Citus, CockroachDB scale SQL
- 'NoSQL has no schema' — your app has one; just implicit. Formalize with JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf
- 'NoSQL means no joins' — MongoDB `$lookup`, DynamoDB streams; usually denormalized at write time
- 'NoSQL is cheaper' — depends; Cassandra needs DBA expertise; DynamoDB expensive at high volume

**Watch for:**
- Denormalization means writes propagate to many documents; painful if source data churns
- Access-pattern lock-in — DynamoDB/Cassandra schemas encode access patterns; new query often = redesign
- Sharding hotspots from monotonic keys — use ULID/UUID or composite keys

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four NoSQL families** — key-value, document, wide-column, graph — each serves specific access patterns
- **CAP is partition-time** — PACELC captures the daily latency-vs-consistency trade-off
- **Tunable consistency is the practical answer** — Cassandra levels, DynamoDB strong-reads, MongoDB concerns
- **BASE complements ACID** — modern systems use both; ACID for money, BASE for analytics/cache
- **Quorum math** W + R > N produces strong consistency
- **Postgres in 2026 closes many NoSQL gaps** — JSONB, full-text, geospatial, pgvector
- **Polyglot persistence is the norm** — each store has operational cost; pick by access pattern, not buzzword

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Start with framing**
- NoSQL is four data-model families — key-value, document, wide-column, graph
- Each relaxes a SQL guarantee for horizontal scale, flexible schema, or access-pattern speed

**Explain CAP and PACELC**
- CAP is a partition-time choice — pick Consistency or Availability
- Real systems experience partitions; they pick CP or AP
- PACELC adds: even without partitions, trade Latency vs Consistency
- Cassandra is PA/EL, CockroachDB is PC/EC, DynamoDB default is PA/EL

**Cover tunable consistency**
- Modern NoSQL exposes per-query knobs
- Cassandra consistency levels (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM)
- DynamoDB strong-read opt-in at 2x cost
- MongoDB read/write concerns (majority, linearizable)
- Quorum math — W + R > N produces strong reads

**Close with 2026 pragmatism**
- Start with Postgres — JSONB and extensions cover most needs
- Specialize when access pattern or scale truly demands
- Polyglot persistence is fine; measure, don't guess

questions.question: Deep-dive into CAP theorem and BASE vs ACID — what does each actually guarantee, and how do real systems trade them off?
questions.title: CAP Theorem Deep-Dive and BASE vs ACID
questions.direct_answer: **CAP** states that during a network partition, a distributed system can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance — and since partitions are unavoidable, the real choice is **CP or AP during partition**. **ACID** (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) gives transactional guarantees ideal for money movement; **BASE** (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) trades those guarantees for scale and availability. Modern systems mix both — ACID for orders/payments, BASE for counters/caches. MongoDB 4.0+ adds multi-document transactions, DynamoDB supports `TransactWriteItems` up to 100 items, and across services the **saga pattern** with outbox + compensating actions replaces distributed two-phase commit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can precisely state CAP and ACID guarantees, and explain BASE as a deliberate trade-off rather than a weakness
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing CAP's 'Consistency' (linearizability) with ACID's 'Consistency' (constraint preservation), or treating BASE as 'no guarantees at all'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show saga-vs-2PC pattern, discuss MongoDB multi-doc transactions since 4.0, and explain why CAP's C ≠ ACID's C

sections.title: CAP, ACID, BASE — Precise Definitions
sections.content:
**CAP** (Eric Brewer, 2000) applies to distributed systems during a network partition.
- You pick at most two of: **Consistency** (every read sees latest write), **Availability** (every request returns a response), **Partition tolerance** (system operates despite network failure).
- In practice P is mandatory, so choose CP or AP during partition.

**ACID** is a single-node transactional contract — **Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability** — with 'Consistency' meaning constraint preservation (FK, uniqueness), not CAP's linearizability. A transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another.

**BASE** is the NoSQL philosophy: **Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent**. It trades strict guarantees for availability, scale, and latency — the right call for caches, feeds, analytics, and counters, and the wrong call for payments.

sections.title: ACID in Practice
sections.content:
**Atomicity**
- All statements in a transaction commit together or none do
- Crash mid-transaction → automatic rollback
- Implemented via write-ahead log (WAL) in Postgres/MySQL

**Consistency (ACID sense)**
- Transaction preserves DB invariants — FK, CHECK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL
- Different from CAP's Consistency (which is linearizability across replicas)

**Isolation**
- Concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate state
- Levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable
- Postgres default: Read Committed; Serializable via SSI

**Durability**
- Committed writes survive crash/power loss
- fsync to WAL before ack; replication for disaster survival

```sql
-- Classic ACID example
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'A';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 'B';
-- If either fails, the whole transaction rolls back
COMMIT;
```

sections.title: BASE in Practice
Transactions Across Distributed Systems
ACID vs BASE Side-by-Side
sections.content:
| Dimension | ACID | BASE |
|---|---|---|
| **Consistency** | Strong, immediate | Eventual, bounded delay |
| **Availability** | May reject during contention | Prioritizes response |
| **Scale model** | Vertical (single node) or tight clusters | Horizontal across many nodes |
| **Latency** | Higher — quorum + sync replication | Lower — local write + async replication |
| **Typical use** | Payments, orders, inventory | Counters, feeds, analytics, cache |
| **Failure mode** | Transaction aborts; app retries | Stale reads; reconcile later |
| **Example stores** | Postgres, MySQL, Spanner | Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), Riak |

sections.title: Choosing Per Operation
sections.content:
**When ACID helps:**
- Financial movements, inventory decrements
- Multi-step invariants (reserve seat + charge card)
- Regulatory audit requirements

**When ACID hurts:**
- Cross-region writes — sync replication kills latency
- Very high write throughput beyond single-node capacity
- Loose data where staleness is acceptable

**When BASE helps:**
- View/like/share counters at scale
- Caches, materialized views, search indices
- Cross-service 'facts' where eventual reconcile is fine

**Watch for:**
- Read-your-writes expectations — users expect to see their own write immediately; route reads to primary or use session tokens
- Cache invalidation lag when source-of-truth updates
- 'We'll just use sagas everywhere' — sagas are operationally heavy; use ACID within one store when you can

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CAP forces CP or AP during partition** — P is mandatory, pick C or A
- **CAP's C ≠ ACID's C** — one is linearizability across replicas, the other is constraint preservation
- **ACID is single-node** contract; **BASE is distributed** philosophy
- **Mix both** — ACID for money, BASE for counters/caches
- **MongoDB 4.0+** supports multi-document ACID transactions; use sparingly
- **Saga pattern** replaces 2PC across services — compensating actions, outbox, idempotence
- **Modern NoSQL tunes consistency per query** rather than one global mode

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Define each precisely**
- CAP: during a partition, pick C or A; P is mandatory
- ACID: single-node transaction contract — atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
- BASE: distributed philosophy — basically available, soft state, eventually consistent

**Clarify the C confusion**
- CAP's C is linearizability across replicas
- ACID's C is constraint preservation within a transaction
- Different concepts, same letter

**Give concrete stores**
- ACID strong: Postgres, MySQL, Spanner, MongoDB with majority concerns
- BASE default: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak
- Tunable: most modern NoSQL

**Mention sagas**
- Distributed transactions across services use sagas, not 2PC
- Compensating actions + outbox pattern + idempotence
- Accepts eventual consistency for operational simplicity

questions.question: Explain MongoDB write concern and read concern — how do they tune consistency, durability, and latency per operation?
questions.title: MongoDB Write Concern, Read Concern, and Read Preference
questions.direct_answer: MongoDB exposes three per-operation knobs that together define consistency and durability. **Write concern** (`w`) controls how many replicas must acknowledge a write before the client sees success — `w: 1` is fast, `w: "majority"` is durable. **Read concern** controls what writes a read can see — `local` returns latest including unreplicated, `majority` returns only majority-committed, `linearizable` joins the oplog to guarantee strict recency. **Read preference** routes reads to primary (strong) or secondaries (scalable, may be stale). The production default is `w: majority` + `readConcern: majority` — it survives a single-node failure without losing writes and reads never see uncommitted data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can translate abstract consistency theory into concrete MongoDB operational knobs and justify defaults
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `w: 1` for financial writes, or believing `readPreference: secondary` gives better consistency than primary
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain `linearizable` read concern's oplog-sync cost, mention `readConcern: snapshot` for transactions, and discuss majority write latency under partition

sections.title: Three Knobs, One Consistency Story
sections.content:
MongoDB runs as a **replica set** of 3+ nodes — one primary, the rest secondaries replicating the primary's oplog. All writes go to the primary; reads can go anywhere. To expose choice between **latency, durability, and freshness**, MongoDB gives three per-operation settings.

**Write concern** answers 'how many replicas must ack before I call the write successful'. **Read concern** answers 'how fresh must the data I read be'. **Read preference** answers 'which node do I read from'.

Combining them intelligently — for example `w: "majority"` plus `readConcern: "majority"` — produces **read-your-writes** and durability without paying linearizable cost. The defaults in modern drivers are already `w: majority` for this reason.

sections.title: Write Concern (w, j, wtimeout)
Read Concern (local, majority, linearizable, snapshot)
sections.content:
**`local`** (default outside transactions)
- Returns latest data on queried node, including writes not yet replicated
- Can be rolled back if primary fails — use with care

**`available`**
- Like `local` but on sharded clusters during chunk migration, returns fastest
- May return orphan documents; rarely used

**`majority`**
- Returns only data acknowledged by majority of voting members
- Cannot be rolled back; pairs naturally with `w: majority`
- Typical production default

**`linearizable`**
- Reads only from primary and confirms primary is still the real primary (no split-brain)
- Most expensive; use when strict recency across clients is mandatory
- Only valid for single-document reads

**`snapshot`**
- Consistent view within a multi-document transaction
- Used automatically inside `withTransaction`

```javascript
// Strong: majority-read with majority-write gives read-your-writes
await orders.findOne(
  { _id: 1 },
  { readConcern: { level: "majority" } }
);

// Strictest — read reflects all successfully acknowledged writes
await orders.findOne(
  { _id: 1 },
  { readConcern: { level: "linearizable" } }
);
```

sections.title: Read Preference (where the read goes)
Consistency vs Durability vs Latency Trade-offs
sections.content:
| Write concern | Read concern | Read pref | Consistency | Durability | Latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `w: 0` | `local` | `nearest` | none | weakest | lowest |
| `w: 1` | `local` | `primary` | read-your-writes on primary | lost if primary fails | low |
| `w: majority` | `local` | `secondaryPreferred` | eventual | strong | medium |
| `w: majority` | `majority` | `primary` | read-your-writes | strong | medium-high |
| `w: majority` + `j` | `linearizable` | `primary` | linearizable | strongest | highest |

sections.title: When to Use Each Setting
sections.content:
**When majority write concern helps:**
- Any write you would be upset to lose — orders, payments, user edits
- Multi-document transactions (required inside `withTransaction`)

**When majority hurts:**
- Primary loses quorum → writes block or time out
- Cross-region replica sets — WAN latency multiplies ack time

**When secondary reads help:**
- Analytics, reporting, batch dashboards — stale-by-minutes is fine
- Offloading primary CPU under read-heavy workloads

**Watch for:**
- `w: 1` + failover = silently lost writes
- `readPreference: secondary` + just-inserted-id lookup = 'it disappeared' bugs
- Linearizable reads are single-document only; don't wrap them around aggregation pipelines
- Drivers since MongoDB 3.6 default to `w: majority`; older code may not

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Write concern** governs how many replicas ack before success; `w: majority` is the durable default
- **Read concern** governs freshness; `majority` avoids seeing writes that could roll back
- **Read preference** routes reads; `primary` for strong, `secondary` for offload
- **`w: majority` + `readConcern: majority`** produces read-your-writes cheaply
- **Linearizable** is single-doc only and most expensive; use sparingly
- **`maxStalenessSeconds`** prevents reads from lagging secondaries
- **Transactions** auto-use `snapshot` read concern and require `w: majority`

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Three knobs**
- Write concern — how many replicas ack before success
- Read concern — how fresh must the read be
- Read preference — which node serves the read

**Production defaults**
- `w: majority` so writes survive a node failure
- `readConcern: majority` so reads never see rollback-able data
- `readPreference: primary` for strong; secondary for analytics

**Special modes**
- Linearizable read concern is strongest, single-doc only, most expensive
- Snapshot read concern is used inside multi-document transactions
- `w: 0` is for fire-hose telemetry, never for business data

**Wrap up with the rule**
- `w: majority` + `readConcern: majority` gives read-your-writes without paying linearizable cost — that is why modern drivers default to it
